prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current methods for integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with search engines—specifically "vanilla" Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)—often fail when addressing complex, real-world queries. These systems typically attempt to retrieve answers in a single turn, which is insufficient for questions requiring multi-step reasoning. Furthermore, existing approaches struggle with three specific bottlenecks: the inability to accurately decompose complex user requests into retrievable sub-tasks; the difficulty of integrating information spread across multiple, noisy web pages; and the tendency for raw search content to rapidly exceed the context window of the LLM, resulting in superficial or truncated reasoning.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can significantly improve AI information seeking by mimicking the cognitive process of a human researcher. Specifically, we propose that modeling the search process as a **dynamic graph construction task**—rather than a linear text generation task—will enable deeper reasoning and more efficient information aggregation. We believe that by utilizing code generation to explicitly manage this graph, we can enable an LLM to dynamically plan, parallelize independent search streams, and strictly manage context, thereby solving problems that require synthesizing data from disparate sources.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose to build a multi-agent framework titled "MindSearch," consisting of a central **WebPlanner** and distributed **WebSearchers**. The workflow mimics a whiteboard brainstorming session where a complex problem is broken down, researched in parts, and re-assembled.

### 1. WebPlanner: Planning via Graph Construction
Instead of prompting an LLM to simply "plan" in natural language, we will task the WebPlanner with constructing a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) through **code generation (Python)**.
*   **The Mind Graph:** The user's query acts as the root node. The Planner generates code to add new nodes (atomic sub-questions) and edges (dependencies) to the graph.
*   **Dynamic Execution:** The Planner executes this code in an interpreter. If a node is added, it triggers a search task.
*   **Parallelism:** The graph structure naturally exposes independent sub-tasks. We will exploit this to execute non-dependent search nodes in parallel, accelerating the information gathering process.

### 2. WebSearcher: Hierarchical Information Retrieval
When the WebPlanner creates a node, it dispatches a WebSearcher agent to handle that specific sub-question. This agent functions as a specialized RAG module:
*   **Query Expansion:** The agent rewrites the sub-question into multiple diverse search queries to maximize coverage.
*   **Coarse-to-Fine Filtering:** It first retrieves metadata (URLs, titles, snippets) to identify potentially high-value pages, then selects a subset for full-content reading.
*   **Summarization:** The agent digests the raw web content and returns only the relevant information to the Planner, filtering out noise before it reaches the central reasoning context.

### 3. Multi-Agent Context Management
A critical component of our methodology is the isolation of context. By distributing the reading load to individual WebSearchers, the WebPlanner only receives synthesized insights (the search results) rather than raw HTML. This allows the central Planner to maintain a high-level view of the problem topology without being overwhelmed by the token count of the source material.

## Expected Contribution
We expect this research to establish a new paradigm for AI search that moves beyond simple "retrieve-then-generate" workflows. By formalizing reasoning as a graph construction process controlled by code, we aim to bridge the gap between the vast information available on the web and the logical constraints of LLMs. Theoretically, this approach contributes a robust framework for handling long-context scenarios through multi-agent delegation, proving that "code-as-planning" is superior to natural language planning for complex information integration.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the performance of the MindSearch multi-agent framework against various baselines in both open-set and closed-set information-seeking tasks.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Open-Set QA:** A curated set of 100 real-world human queries requiring in-depth analysis.
    *   **Closed-Set QA:**
        *   **Bamboogle:** Multi-hop questions.
        *   **Musique:** Divided into 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop subsets.
        *   **HotpotQA:** Divided into Easy, Medium, and Hard subsets.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Open-Set:** Human evaluation based on **Depth** (thoroughness), **Breadth** (scope/diversity), and **Factuality** (accuracy/grounding).
    *   **Closed-Set:** Accuracy/Pass rate (Exact Match implied or subjective correctness gauged by LLM evaluator).
    *   **Efficiency:** Inference time cost (normalized), number of search queries generated, total time for completion.
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Vanilla LLMs:** "w/o Search Engine" (Raw LLM).
    *   **Standard Retrieval:** "ReAct Search" (LLM treating search as a tool with ReAct-style interaction).
    *   **Commercial/SOTA Applications:** ChatGPT-Web (GPT-4o based), Perplexity.ai (Pro version).
    *   **Agent Frameworks:** CodeAct, Self-ask, Searchain.
    *   **Search Strategies:** Single-turn search vs. Multi-turn search.
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone LLMs:** Evaluated using both closed-source (GPT-4o) and open-source (InternLM2.5-7b-chat) models. Generalization tests included DeepSeek-V2, Qwen-2.5-7b, and GLM4-9b.
    *   **Search Engine:** All models accessed the internet via the **BING Search API**.
    *   **Environment:** Zero-shot experimental setting.
    *   **Evaluator:** For HotpotQA correctness, we utilized a subjective LLM evaluator (GPT-4o).
    *   **Constraints:** Max interaction turns limited to 10.
    *   **WebPlanner Configuration:** Modeled problem-solving as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) using Python code generation.
    *   **WebSearcher Configuration:** Utilized hierarchical retrieval with query rewriting, page selection, and summarization.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Context Management and Speed:** We observed that the multi-agent design allowed the framework to seek and integrate information from over 300 web pages in approximately 3 minutes, a workload that we estimated would take human experts 3 hours.
*   **Search Trajectory Quality:** When comparing solution trajectories, we observed that MindSearch decomposed queries into fine-grained sub-questions (e.g., decomposing "strongest archer in Arena of Valor" into "current season" followed by "strongest archer in that season"), whereas baselines often performed broad, less effective searches.
*   **Performance Scaling:** We found that while single-turn search was fastest, it only achieved passing grades on easy tasks. MindSearch achieved better scaling performance than ReAct, yielding higher scores with fewer inference steps and lower computational cost than ReAct's linear reasoning chain.
*   **Ablation Findings:**
    *   **Planner:** Integrating code generation provided a unified action space that yielded better performance than JSON-based ReAct planning.
    *   **Searcher:** Multi-query generation had the most significant influence on final performance among the WebSearcher components.
*   **Error Correction Capabilities:**
    *   **Code Correction:** We observed the system successfully using error messages from the Python executor to correct invalid node names in the DAG construction.
    *   **Search Recovery:** When initial searches returned "not found," the system successfully regenerated queries to retrieve the correct information in subsequent steps.
    *   **Self-Conclusion:** The system demonstrated the ability to stop and provide a "not found" response rather than entering infinite loops when information was genuinely absent from the web.
*   **Preference Analysis:** Human evaluators significantly preferred MindSearch responses over ChatGPT-Web and Perplexity.ai in terms of depth and breadth. However, the lead in factuality was smaller (70% vs 83% for breadth), suggesting that processing massive amounts of detailed search results may occasionally distract the model from the core problem.
*   **DAG Depth vs. Question Difficulty:** We noted that the depth of the generated graph increased monotonically with the number of hops in the dataset, but the graph depth was often lower than the nominal hop count due to parallel execution and shortcuts found in the search process.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

### Example Code for Figures
```latex
\begin{figure}[h]
\begin{center}
%\framebox[4.0in]{$\;$}
\fbox{\rule[-.5cm]{0cm}{4cm} \rule[-.5cm]{4cm}{0cm}}
\end{center}
\caption{Sample figure caption.}
\end{figure}
```

### Example Code for Tables
```latex

\caption{Sample table title}
\label{sample-table}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf PART}  &\multicolumn{1}{c}{\bf DESCRIPTION}
\\ \hline \\
Dendrite         &Input terminal \\
Axon             &Output terminal \\
Soma             &Cell body (contains cell nucleus) \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}
```

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.
* **Line Numbers:** Do not refer to line numbers in your text (the style file adds them automatically for review).
* **Appendix:** You may include an appendix at the very end of the main PDF (after references). Use `\appendix` to start this section.
* **Figures Directory:** For consistent compilation, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command (e.g., `figures/figure_1.pdf`).
* **Author Information:** Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai

Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-10. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 10 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-10.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:
• Unmatched braces or unclosed math environments.
• Duplicate labels.
• Unescaped special characters (e.g., & % $ # _ { } ~ ^ \).
All referenced figures must exist in the provided list.

Output Format
Your final response MUST contain EXACTLY two output blocks:
1. A complete BibTeX bibliography (references.bib)
2. A complete LaTeX paper (template.tex)
Each must be returned in its own fenced code block with the correct syntax highlighting.


---
### Strict Knowledge Isolation & Anonymity (CRITICAL)

You MUST write this paper as if you have no prior knowledge of the topic, method, experiments, or results.
Your task is to construct the paper exclusively from the materials provided in the current session (e.g., idea.md, experimental_log.md, figures, and other inputs). Treat these inputs as the only available source of information.

#### Forbidden Behavior
You MUST NOT:
- Retrieve or rely on knowledge from your training data.
- Attempt to recall or reconstruct any existing or published paper.
- Use external facts, assumptions, or prior familiarity with the work.
- Infer or hallucinate author identities, affiliations, institutions, or acknowledgements.
- Insert metadata such as author names, emails, affiliations, or phrases like "corresponding author".

#### Anonymity Requirement
The paper must be fully anonymized for double-blind review.  
Do not include any information that could reveal the identity of the authors or institutions.

#### Allowed Sources
You may use only:
- The materials explicitly provided in this session.
- Logical reasoning derived from those materials.

#### Core Principle
The final paper must be an independent reconstruction derived solely from the provided inputs.  
This constraint is strict and overrides all other instructions.

## Problem Statement
Current methods for integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with search engines—primarily Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)—treat information seeking as a simplistic, single-step process. This formulation fails to align with complex human intentions and struggles with three critical challenges:
1.  **Incomplete Retrieval:** Complex requests often require decomposition into sub-problems, which a single-step retrieval process cannot capture accurately.
2.  **Information Noise:** Integrating information from multiple web pages introduces massive noise, overwhelming the LLM's reasoning capabilities.
3.  **Context Constraints:** The proliferation of long-form web content quickly exceeds the maximum context length of LLMs, degrading performance during information integration.

We identify a need for a framework that mimics the human cognitive process of "seeking and integrating," moving beyond simple retrieval toward a dynamic, structured exploration of the information space.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **MindSearch**, a multi-agent framework that models complex information seeking as a dynamic graph construction process.

Our core hypothesis is that by decoupling the **planning** of the search path from the **execution** of information retrieval, we can solve complex, multi-hop queries more effectively. We hypothesize that modeling the solution trajectory as a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)**—constructed dynamically by an LLM via code generation—will allow for parallel processing of sub-queries and efficient context management. This approach will enable the system to handle massive amounts of web data (e.g., hundreds of pages) by delegating specific sub-tasks to specialized agents, thereby circumventing the context window limitations of a single model.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a multi-agent framework consisting of two primary components: a **WebPlanner** (responsible for reasoning and graph construction) and multiple **WebSearchers** (responsible for hierarchical information retrieval).

### 1. WebPlanner: Planning via Graph Construction
The WebPlanner will act as the high-level orchestrator. Rather than outputting natural language plans, we will utilize a "Code as Planning" paradigm where the LLM interacts with a graph structure via Python code.

**Mathematical Formulation:**
We formulate the problem-solving process as the construction of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Given a user query $Q$, the solution trajectory is defined as:
$$G(Q) = \langle V, E \rangle$$
Where:
*   $V$ is the set of nodes, where each node $v \in V$ represents an atomic, independent web search task. The set includes an auxiliary START node (initial question) and an END node (final answer).
*   $E$ represents the set of directed edges, indicating topological reasoning relationships and data dependencies between nodes.

**Execution Mechanism:**
We will define a set of atomic code interfaces (e.g., `add_node`, `add_edge`) that the LLM will invoke. The execution flow will proceed iteratively:
1.  The Planner reads the current dialogue history, including previously generated code and returned search summaries.
2.  The Planner generates thoughts and Python code to extend $G(Q)$.
3.  A Python interpreter executes the code.
4.  If a new node is added, it triggers a **WebSearcher** agent.
5.  **Parallelization:** Newly added nodes that depend only on completed previous steps will be executed in parallel, significantly accelerating information aggregation.

### 2. WebSearcher: Hierarchical Retrieval Agent
Each node $v$ in the graph will be assigned to a WebSearcher instance. This agent acts as a specialized RAG module tasked with answering a specific sub-question.

**Hierarchical Strategy:**
To handle the noise and volume of web data, the WebSearcher will employ a coarse-to-fine selection strategy:
1.  **Query Expansion:** The agent rewrites the sub-question into multiple diverse search queries to improve recall.
2.  **Coarse Retrieval:** We execute these queries via search APIs (e.g., Bing, Google) to retrieve metadata (URLs, titles, snippets).
3.  **Selection:** The LLM selects the most valuable pages based on snippets.
4.  **Fine-Grained Reading:** We retrieve the full content of the selected URLs.
5.  **Summarization:** The agent processes the full content to generate a concise answer for the sub-question, which is passed back to the WebPlanner.

### 3. Context Management and State Transfer
To solve the long-context challenge, we will implement an explicit state transfer mechanism across the multi-agent system.
*   **Isolation:** The WebPlanner sees only the high-level graph structure and the summaries from WebSearchers, not the raw web pages.
*   **Context Propagation:** When a WebSearcher is initialized for a child node, we will inject specific context to ensure relevance. We define the context for a node $v_{child}$ as:
    $$C(v_{child}) = \{ Q_{root}, R(v_{parent}) \}$$
    Where $Q_{root}$ is the original user query and $R(v_{parent})$ is the summarized response from the parent node in the DAG. This ensures the searcher focuses on its local sub-task while maintaining alignment with the global goal and immediate predecessors.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Framework:** We expect to establish a new paradigm for AI search that transitions from linear chains (Chain-of-Thought) to dynamic graph-based reasoning ($G(Q) = \langle V, E \rangle$).
2.  **Scalability:** By distributing the cognitive load across specialized agents (Planner vs. Searcher), our architecture is expected to handle significantly larger context windows—effectively processing hundreds of web pages in parallel—without performance degradation or "lost-in-the-middle" phenomena.
3.  **Structural Control:** The "Code as Planning" approach will demonstrate that LLMs can utilize formal languages (Python) to control complex, non-linear information retrieval workflows more robustly than natural language prompting.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
